title: The side of the room that disappears

blocks.text: The side of the room that disappears

AMaC MRCP PACES · R5-172 · Neurological examination · PACES Station 3, neurological examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 minutes (up to 6 examination, at least 4 questions) · Guideline dates and links in section 15 · Related AMaC: condition may appear elsewhere in a different context

Dear Doctor, examine attention, visual function and relevant neurological signs in a man aged 67, four months after a stroke. He keeps colliding with objects on his left. Distinguish a visual field defect from inattention and discuss the functional implications. He can sit unsupported; please do not ask him to walk without assistance.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: HOOK: Seeing a left stimulus alone but missing it during bilateral stimulation points to extinction.
TRAP: Neglect, homonymous hemianopia and weakness can coexist; do not use one label to explain every missed stimulus.

rows: Check the conditions of the test.
“Can you see this clearly, and are your glasses comfortable?”
Establish alertness, language comprehension and acuity before interpreting attention.
Test each side separately before both together.
“Tell me whether you see movement on the left, right, or both.”
Assess visual fields with maintained fixation, then bilateral simultaneous visual and sensory stimulation.
Look for neglect in ordinary tasks.
“Please describe everything around you on this table.”
Assess left-sided exploration, line bisection or cancellation using a clearly specified task.
“The problem may affect scanning, eating and moving around.”
Arrange occupational therapy, rehabilitation and vision assessment; discuss driving and home risk.
Adapts positioning to reduce competing cues and documents test limitations.
Tests left and right alone before simultaneous stimulation.
Demonstrates visual extinction while keeping fixation under observation.
Finds left neglect on a second task.
Separates visual, tactile and personal inattention where relevant.
Localises the problem to the left eye.
Identifies a right hemispheric attentional syndrome.
Distinguishes parietal network dysfunction from isolated primary visual-field loss.
Recommends independent walking practice without assessment.
Plans OT-led safety and rehabilitation input.
Links scanning strategies to the patient’s actual home and meal tasks.
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): tells him to restart driving because acuity is normal.
Advises against driving pending appropriate assessment and licensing advice.
Considers insight, falls, carer involvement with consent and recurrent stroke symptoms.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade.
Skills: A physical examination; B identifying physical signs; C clinical communication; D differential diagnosis; E clinical judgement; F managing patients’ concerns; G maintaining patient welfare.

Patient: a retired bus mechanic. A right middle cerebral artery stroke four months ago affected your left arm and awareness. You feel your sight is “fine”, but your daughter says you eat mainly from the right side of the plate and catch the left doorframe. No new episode, headache or sudden decline. Your prescribed medicines are clopidogrel, atorvastatin and amlodipine; dosing is reviewed by the stroke clinic. No known drug allergies.

You walk with a stick and supervision outside. You have not driven since the stroke. Hidden concern: you resent needing help in your own kitchen. Opening: “The furniture seems to get in my way.” If challenged bluntly, become defensive; if shown the difference between one stimulus and two, acknowledge that you missed the left one. For any cancellation or bisection task the examiner supplies a consistent written result; no screenshot or unseen image is required.

Findings and delivery. Alert, fluent speech and intact comprehension. Corrected acuity is 6/9 each eye; pupils equal and reactive. On controlled confrontation he detects single stimuli in each hemifield. With bilateral simultaneous visual stimulation he repeatedly reports only the right stimulus. The same left extinction occurs with simultaneous touch to the hands. Cancellation task: identifies nearly all targets on the right and leaves most left-sided targets; line midpoint marked to the right of true centre. Mild left arm pyramidal weakness and brisker left reflexes are present. These findings support a broader right hemispheric stroke with parietal attention-network involvement, not an anatomically pure small parietal lesion. No complete new field deficit is supplied.

Question ladder. Q1 (R2) What is extinction? Detection of a single contralateral stimulus is preserved but it is missed when an ipsilateral stimulus competes simultaneously. Q2 (R4) How does that differ from hemianopia? A true field loss affects a consistent region even with single stimuli. Neglect is an attentional disorder, although both can coexist. Q3 (R4) Where is the lesion? The right hemispheric attention network, commonly involving parietal regions; the additional motor findings fit the supplied wider stroke. Q4 (R5) How would you help at meals? OT assessment, scanning/attention strategies, environmental adjustments and support tailored to observed eating and mobility difficulties. Q5 (R6) What if this started this morning? Activate the acute stroke pathway immediately rather than conducting a chronic rehabilitation consultation.
Compares single with double stimulation (A B).
Corroborates inattention with a different task (B).
Uses the findings to distinguish attention from primary vision (D).
Recognises that poor insight affects safety and rehabilitation (E G).
Fail performance
CANDIDATE waves both hands at once and declares a left homonymous hemianopia without single-stimulus testing. [R2 Fail R3 Fail] “Your eyes are fine, so driving is fine.” [R6 Fail]
Pass performance

CANDIDATE establishes single-stimulus detection then demonstrates left visual and tactile extinction. [R2 Pass] “This is left-sided inattention after a right hemispheric stroke.” [R4 Pass] Plans OT and supervised mobility. [R5 Pass]
High-performance performance

CANDIDATE explains the discrepancy using the patient’s meal difficulty, avoids blaming him for lack of awareness and offers an achievable kitchen task for rehabilitation. [R3 High R5 High R6 High] EXAMINER: distinguishes the syndromes and makes the finding useful to the patient.
R2: Without single-sided testing, extinction cannot be distinguished from field loss.
R4: Right brain disease causes the supplied left attention problem; the left eye is not the localisation.
R6: Normal acuity alone does not establish fitness to drive.
“I should test each side alone before comparing both together.”
“This may be a problem of attention rather than the eye itself.”
“Let us relate the result to what happens at home.”

Neglect is a failure to orient or respond appropriately to the opposite side of space or the body. It is not equivalent to hemianopia or deliberate inattention. Bedside assessment should use more than one task, account for language and visual limitations, and connect findings to daily activities. Rehabilitation planning needs a team assessment, including occupational therapy and appropriate vision expertise. Acute recurrence must be treated as possible new stroke, even in someone with an established disability.
THINK: Single stimuli first, competing stimuli second.
SAY: “You can detect the left side alone, but it is missed when both sides compete.”
DO: Fields, extinction, cancellation and functional assessment.
NUMBERS: No bisection cut-off is invented for a bedside task.
TRAP: Equating neglect with blindness.
FINISH: OT, environmental safety, driving assessment and secondary prevention review.
